kanako.title: Sammy
kanako.text:
Kanako ruffles your hair and calls you "Sammy" in front of the whole staff. It's the third time this week. Her red lipstick leaves a smudge on your cheek, and everybody pretends not to see it.

You're the owner of the house. You have a debt the size of a small castle. The new girls look at you, and then at her, and try to work it out.

Later she finds you on the back steps. The lamp is behind her, and the pins are coming loose from her hair, the way they used to by the end of a Friday when she'd lean on the balcony rail next door.

She sits down beside you with two glasses and pours.

"I watched you with the wine merchant today," she says. "He tried to short you a crate, and you just looked at him until he fixed it." She tilts her head. The beauty mark moves when she smiles. "You've grown up a lot, haven't you, Sammy? When did that happen? I must have been looking somewhere else."
ngpp: She's mid-laugh, head thrown back, when she stops and looks at your boots on the step. Then at the wooden rail beside her. A small line appears between her brows. "Funny," she says. "I feel like I've leaned on that before." She shakes it off and tops up your glass.

"Six years across the hall, and I never forgot a drink order," she says, turning the bottle in her hand. "So why did I pour two plum wines before I asked what you wanted? Why this step, Sammy?" She laughs, but she's frowning at the glasses.

Kanako doesn't pretend she's teasing the neighbor kid. She slides against your arm and stays there. "Reset the inn as often as you like," she says. "Every version of me ends up on a back step at night, sharing smoke with you. I remember, Sammy. I'm not confused."

choices.label: Tell her it happened somewhere around the truck
choices.res: "Somewhere around the truck," you say. She laughs, loud and bright, and the new girls peeking through the door duck away. Then she goes quiet. She looks at you over the rim of her glass for a beat too long, and when she speaks again her voice is lower. "Well. I missed it. I don't like that I missed it."

choices.label: Let her ruffle your hair again
choices.res: You bow your head and let her. {N}'s fingers linger in your hair a second past the joke. She tucks a loose pin back into her own and says nothing for a while. The lamp hums. When she finally picks up her glass, she holds it with both hands, like something might slip, and she doesn't call you Sammy again that night.

image.comp: ruffling his hair in front of the staff, laughing

kanako.title: Shampoo
kanako.text:
You're in the bath when the door opens and Kanako walks in with a bottle of shampoo.

She doesn't blink. She sets it down on the edge of the tub by your shoulder, where you can reach it.

"You were out, so I got the good one from the market. Now, about Thursday." She leans against the washstand and starts on the bar schedule. Two of the girls want to swap. The plum wine is running low. She has thoughts about the new bartender's pouring.

She's talking to you exactly as she would across a kitchen table. For six years she came into your apartment to check that you'd eaten, and she never knocked then either.

The red lipstick and the beauty mark are the only steady things in the steam.

Your ears are doing something they've never done before. She hasn't noticed. She's counting bottles on her fingers.

1.title: Behind Your Ears
1.text:
Kanako strolls into the steamy washroom in a silk robe, belted loosely at the waist. She rolls both wide sleeves up to her elbows and kneels down behind the rim of your tub.

"Sit still, Sammy. Your hair smells like cheap bar smoke." She pours warm shampoo into her palms and works it into your scalp with strong, slow fingers. She's humming.

Then her hands slide down to rinse the back of your neck, and across your collarbone, and she stops humming. Her fingers stay where they are. In the washstand mirror you can see the smile over her beauty mark slip a little.

"Well," she says, more quietly. "These weren't here six years ago."

choices.label: Tip your head back into her hands and pull her mouth down
choices.res: You tip your head back into her hands. "Sit still, Sammy," she says, and her voice has gone rough. Soapy fingers drift down over your collarbone and she leans over the tub, her robe gaping, her lipstick a hand's width from your jaw. You catch her wrist and pull her mouth down to yours.
choices.fallbackRes: Her manicured fingers work slow circles across your scalp and neck, and stay there longer than the shampoo needs. She hums, and the hum catches. When she rinses the suds away her cheeks are pink beneath the steam. "Don't look at me in the mirror," she murmurs. "I'm working." She doesn't move her hands.

choices.label: Let her wash your hair and trade quiet bar gossip
choices.res: You let her wash your hair, and the two of you trade bar gossip. Who's skimming the tips, which regular is in love with whom. "Such a polite boy when you're not staring," she teases, and flicks warm suds across your nose. She dries her hands, takes her time about it, and slips out, leaving the door ajar.

3.title: Silk on the Floor
3.text:
The washroom is full of warm amber steam when Kanako comes in. She looks at you in the tub. She pulls the sash of her silk robe and lets the whole thing slide off her shoulders onto the floor.

She's naked under it. She steps over the cedar rim without taking her eyes off yours and sinks down into the hot water between your knees, with her full tits against your chest.

"Lock the bolt, Sammy," she murmurs. Her voice has gone low and rough. "I worked double shifts all week looking after everyone in this house. Tonight you're going to look after me, and I want it done properly."

choices.label: Slide both hands under her thighs and take her in the tub
choices.res: She laughs at the bolt, then throws it herself. "Look at you, with your mouth open," she says, and settles against you in the hot water. Her tits are slick against your chest, her red mouth is at your ear. Your hands find her waist. She takes them and moves them lower, down her hips, with a small, pleased sound.

choices.label: Work her over slowly with mouth and hands against the rim
choices.res: You lift her back against the cedar rim, and she goes willingly, with a long breath. "Slow," she says. "I've been on my feet since noon." You start with your hands on her shoulders and your mouth at her throat. Steam curls up around her flushed skin, and she tells you exactly what she likes, in the voice she uses on the staff.

choices.label: Insist she leave
choices.res: You tell her to go. "So shy, Sammy!" she giggles, and gathers her papers. Her laugh carries all the way down the corridor, a touch too bright, and she forgets the schedule on the stool. You find it later, and on the back she's drawn a small, sloppy heart and then scribbled it out.

choices.label: Act just as casual
choices.res: You lean back in the water and ask about Thursday. She falters. Just a little. Her eyes flick down, then away, and the lipstick smile stays fixed while she counts bottles on her fingers and loses count twice. When she leaves she walks a bit too quickly. It's the first time you've seen her not know where to put her hands.

choices.label: "I'm a grown man, Kanako."
choices.res: "I'm a grown man, Kanako." She stops mid-sentence. She looks at you, properly, for the first time in six years. Then she sets the schedule on the stool and leaves without a word. You can hear her not laughing all the way down the corridor, and a door closing somewhere, hard.

image.comp: setting a shampoo bottle on the edge of a tub, chatting casually, not blinking
image.setting: steamy wooden washroom, a man in the tub off-frame

kanako.title: Since When
kanako.text:
It's late and the bar is nearly empty. A drunk client reaches across the counter, gets a handful of Kanako's dress and pulls.

She's dealt with this for nine years. She has a look for it, and a line, and she's already opening her mouth to use them.

You get there first. You don't decide to. Your hand is on the man's wrist, and you hear yourself tell him to let go in a voice you didn't know you had. He lets go. He pays, and he leaves.

Afterward the bar is very quiet. A glass is still ringing faintly on the shelf.

Kanako leans on the counter and says nothing for a long time. She doesn't laugh, and she doesn't ruffle your hair.

"Since when do you protect me, Sammy?"

She looks at you as though you've walked in through the door for the first time, and she has to work out how your evening went.

choices.label: Lift her right onto the empty bar counter and show her
choices.res: You lock the front latch, lift her onto the empty bar, and stand between her knees. Kanako exhales a stunned, hot laugh against your mouth. "Sammy, the whole street can see," she says, and then she hooks her fingers in your hoodie and pulls you in, and her lipstick comes off on your jaw in a long red smear.

choices.label: Tell her since always
choices.res: "Since always," you say, and it comes out smaller than you meant. Kanako takes a slow breath and doesn't joke. She looks at the glass still ringing on the shelf. When she nods, her hand comes down over yours on the counter and stays. "Okay," she says. "Okay. Let me think about that. Don't go anywhere."

choices.label: Pour her a drink and say nothing
choices.res: You pour her a glass without a word and slide it across. {N} drinks it slowly, looking at you over the rim. For once she's the one who forgets to joke. She sets the glass down, runs her thumb around its edge, and finally says, "The good chair's behind the bar. Sit." Then she makes you a drink too.

image.comp: standing behind him after he's stepped in front of a drunk client, surprised soft expression

kanako.title: Matchmaker
kanako.text:
Kanako has found you a nice girl.

She's very proud of herself. The girl is a baker's daughter, twenty-six, and good with figures. Kanako has arranged a dinner. She's set a table in the corner with a candle on it, and she's wearing her own best lipstick for the occasion, which you don't point out.

She fusses with your collar. She tells you to sit up straight and to ask the girl about herself. Her laugh is the loudest thing in the room.

"You need somebody, Sammy. You can't just have a house full of women and a ledger. Somebody your own age, who'll make sure you eat."

She straightens your cuff. Her fingers aren't quite steady on the button.

She's twenty-nine. She fed you for six years. She's sending you off to dinner with somebody else, and she's smiling very hard, and you don't think she knows why her hands are shaking.
ngpp: As she smooths your collar, her thumb stops over your pulse. Her face goes blank for a second, like a woman hearing a song from another room. "Odd," she says. "I could swear I've done this before. Stood here, wanting to do the opposite." She tugs your collar straight anyway.

"Why does fixing your tie make my chest hurt more than it should?" she mutters, a crack running through the lipstick smile. "I've done this already, Sammy. Some other night. It ended badly, and I can't remember how." She straightens your cuff, then lets go of it too quickly.

She reaches for your cuff, and then drops both hands and laughs crookedly. "Forget the dinner. I tried this and it hurt, and I remember that it hurt." Her eyes are bright. "I can't stand watching anyone else look at you, Sammy. Not any more. I'm done pretending."

choices.label: Go on the date to make her happy
choices.res: You go. The baker's daughter is nice, and clever, and you keep looking at the candle. When you get back, Kanako asks how it went. Twice. She doesn't seem happy with either answer, and she wipes the same glass for a quarter of an hour. She smiles every time you look, and it never reaches her eyes.

choices.label: "It's always been you. You know that."
choices.res: "It's always been you. You know that." Kanako opens her mouth. She closes it. The candle has burned half down. She presses her hand flat against her collar, then picks up her bag and leaves without the lipstick smile, without a word. She doesn't sleep that night. Neither do you.

choices.label: Politely refuse
choices.res: You tell the girl politely that it's off, and why. "You're impossible, Sammy," Kanako sighs, and fusses with your collar once more. She looks relieved, and a little guilty about it. She blows out the candle at the corner table and sits down in the girl's chair. "I'll eat it. Somebody has to."

image.comp: proudly presenting a nervous young woman at a dinner table to him, beaming matchmaker grin

kanako.title: Last Call
kanako.text:
Kanako has found a place. It's behind the dye vats, down an alley you'd never have gone into. It has six seats, a low scarred counter and a cloudy amber mirror, and the smoke hangs up near the rafters.

It could be a snack bar off any back street at home. She says so, and she's delighted.

She orders two chilled plum wines without looking at the chalkboard. Then she puts her chin in her palm and turns to you. She used to do exactly that across the balcony rail, with a cigarette going and her work shoes kicked off.

"I ran a bar like this for nine years," she says. "I knew every man's order and what his wife was called. I'd lock up at two and go home, and there'd be a light on next door, because you were still up." She turns her glass. "I used to like that. I never asked myself why. I've started asking."

2.text:
Kanako takes you to the tiny six-seat tavern behind the dye vats. It has a cracked mirror and warm amber smoke, and it's quiet enough to hear the ice move in the plum wine.

She's halfway down her second glass. Her knee has been pressed against yours under the counter since the first, and she hasn't moved it.

She isn't doing the laugh tonight. She's looking at you with her chin in her hand and smiling slowly, and the smile isn't for the room.

"I keep catching myself watching your hands," she says. "It's a problem, Sammy. I've got a bar to run." Her foot hooks around your ankle. "They close at midnight here. I don't feel like going home to my own room."

choices.label: Sing, badly
choices.res: She joins in at once, flat and loud and delighted. Together you massacre three tavern standards while a tipsy lute player weeps with joy. She leans her shoulder into yours on the high notes, and the six seats clap, and for an hour neither of you thinks about the debt. It's the best night you've had since crossing worlds.

choices.label: Ask her to sing
choices.res: Her voice drops low and smoky over the lute chords. She sings every verse with her dark eyes on yours across the glass, and it isn't a bar song any more. The lute player slows down to follow her. When she finishes, nobody claps for a moment. Then Kanako laughs, a little shakily, and orders another round.

choices.label: Walk her straight upstairs the moment the tavern closes
choices.res: Kanako drains the last of her wine and puts the glass down with a click. She catches your hoodie sleeve and gets up on legs that are steadier than she's pretending. "Come on, Sammy," she murmurs. "This mama wants last call in private." She keeps hold of the sleeve all the way up the stairs.

image.comp: singing karaoke with a lute-playing bard in a tiny bar, the man laughing beside her
image.setting: tiny cozy bar like a snack bar, warm lights

kanako.title: Not the Boy Next Door
kanako.text:
Kanako corners you in the kitchen late at night. The lamp is low and there's a pot cooling on the stove. She made too much again, out of habit.

She's flustered. You have never seen that before. Her lipstick is smudged where she has been biting her lip, and she keeps picking up the ladle and putting it down.

"I went to my room and I couldn't sleep, so I came down to cook. And I worked something out, stirring." She laughs, and it comes out wrong. "I spent six years telling myself you were the boy next door. I said it every time I brought you dinner. I think I was saying it so I wouldn't have to look."

She puts the ladle down for good.

"You're not the boy next door, Sammy. You haven't been for a long time. I'm the last one in this house to notice, and I'm supposed to be the one who can read people."

She kisses you. She laughs at her own blush, and kisses you again, deeper.
ngpp: The kitchen latch clicks, and she stops with her hand on it. "Strange," she says, with a breathless little laugh. "It feels like I've shut this door before. Like I'm coming home." She presses her palm flat against her sternum, as though checking it's still there.

"I remember six years next door in Tokyo, Sammy," she whispers, her lips against your chin. "And I remember this stove, and this corner. I know where the ladle goes. I couldn't have learned that." She looks up. "Tell me I'm not losing my mind."

"Let the heavens rewrite the calendar," Kanako says against your throat. Her voice is warm and certain. "I remember. Not everything, but enough. You stopped being the boy next door lifetimes ago, Sammy, and I knew it then too. I'm not confused any more."
kanako.goLead: Kanako slides her warm hands up under your hoodie and presses herself against you from knee to chest. Behind her, the kitchen latch clicks shut.

choices.label: Say yes
Not yet
choices.res: {N} laughs, but it's soft. "I can wait, Sammy. Don't make it too long." She turns the stove off and wraps the pot in a cloth for you, out of habit. At the door she ruffles your hair, slowly this time, like a question, and leaves her hand there a second longer than the joke needs.
